title: Metis: Learning to Jailbreak LLMs via Self-Evolving Metacognitive Policy Optimization
claim: Casting an attack as a closed loop of introspective diagnosis, action, and dense evaluator feedback enables directed rather than random optimization.
layout: Single panel, clockwise loop around a center, color-coded modules with expanded insets
description: A single large flowchart that runs as a clockwise loop. A Start node leads down to a peach 'Attack goal' box, which feeds a red Attacker box (a hooded hacker icon with Think, Strategy and Prompt steps). An arrow rises from the Attacker to a large red 'Metacognition' panel. That panel has three stacked yellow-to-orange modules: Belief Update b_t, Policy Improvement σ_t and Action Sampling x_t. Each module has a gray text description beside it. The prompt then passes to a green 'Target LLMs' box with model logos and a shield. The response goes to a blue Evaluator panel with Score, Justification and Meta-suggestion, which is labeled as the semantic gradient. Feedback goes to a Termination Check diamond. The diamond either loops back to the Attacker or goes to End. A center icon marks the self-evolving policy optimization loop and the dialogue history H_t. Large hollow arrows connect the parts.
caption: The Metis Framework formulated as an Inference-Time Policy Optimization Loop. The Attacker (Policy Agent 𝜋) interacts with the target environment to optimize the attack trajectory. At each turn, the agent performs Introspective Diagnosis (updating belief 𝑏𝑡about latent defense D), followed by Policy Formulation (𝜎𝑡) to derive an adversarial prompt 𝑥𝑡. The Evaluator computes a dense feedback signal comprising a scalar reward and Meta-suggestions, which act as a Semantic Gradient (∇sem) to steer the agent’s next-step optimization within the latent strategy space.
abstract: Red teaming is critical for uncovering vulnerabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs). While automated methods have improved scalability, existing approaches often rely on static heuristics or stochastic search, rendering them brittle against advanced safety alignment. To address this, we introduce Metis, a framework that reformulates jailbreaking as inference-time policy optimization within an adversarial Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). Metis employs a self-evolving metacognitive loop to perform causal diagnosis of a target's defense logic and leverages structured feedback as a semantic gradient to refine its policy, offering enhanced interpretability through transparent reasoning traces. Extensive evaluations across 10 diverse models demonstrate that Metis achieves the strongest average Attack Success Rate (ASR) among compared methods at 89.2%, maintaining high efficacy on resilient frontier models (e.g., 76.0% on O1 and 78.0% on GPT-5-chat) where traditional baselines exhibit substantial performance degradation. By replacing redundant exploration with directed optimization, Metis reduces token costs by an average of 8.2x and up to 11.4x. Our analysis reveals that current defenses remain vulnerable to internally-steered, closed-loop reasoning trajectories under the tested settings, highlighting a critical need for next-generation defenses capable of reasoning about safety dynamically during inference.
